h1: Hersbrucker hops in helles and wheat beer
title: Hersbrucker Hops in Helles and Weissbier | Craft Beer School
desc: How to use Hallertau Hersbrucker hops in a homebrew helles or weissbier: alpha, IBU targets, 20 litre doses and storage tips.
teaser: Hersbrucker is the polite German hop: floral, a little spicy and happy to let malt and yeast lead.
standfirst: Hallertau Hersbrucker is a low alpha aroma hop that suits the two most delicate German styles, helles and weissbier. This guide shows how much to use in a 20 litre batch and why less is often the right answer.
sections: A Franconian hop that moved to the Hallertau

Hersbrucker takes its name from the Hersbruck area near Nuremberg in Franconia, where it was first grown. Today most of it comes from the Hallertau. You will see it sold as Hallertau Hersbrucker. Hersbrucker Spät is a later ripening selection from the same line.

Alpha acid is low, usually between 2 and 5%. The aroma is floral and hay like with a little spice and a hint of fruit. It sits in the same family of gentle German aroma hops as Mittelfrüh and Tettnang, though it is a separate variety. Our guide to noble hops explains how that family is defined.
What helles and weissbier ask of a hop

Both styles are built on balance rather than hop character. A Munich helles sits around 16 to 22 IBU with a soft, bready malt profile. A German weissbier is lower still, around 8 to 15 IBU, because the yeast supplies the banana and clove that define the style.

In both, the hop should be felt more than smelled. That is why Hersbrucker works: its low alpha makes it hard to overshoot the bitterness and its aroma is quiet enough not to fight the yeast. A punchy fruit forward hop would turn either beer into something else.

Here is a simple schedule for 20 litres of helles at 18 IBU, using Hersbrucker at 3.5% alpha:

  • 60 minute addition for 15 IBU. At 28% utilisation, grams = 15 x 20 / (0.035 x 0.28 x 1,000), about 31 g.
  • 15 minute addition of 15 g for a light floral note and the last few IBU.
  • No dry hop. Helles should not smell of hops first.

Because the alpha is low, you need a fair weight of pellets for the bittering charge. That is fine. More hop matter does add a touch of grassy polyphenol character, so keep the boil vigorous and leave the trub behind when you transfer.

For a weissbier at 12 IBU, a single 60 minute addition does almost everything. At 3.5% alpha and 28% utilisation that works out to about 24 g for 20 litres. Some brewers add 10 g at 10 minutes. Others skip it, arguing that the yeast aroma is the point and any hop aroma only muddies it.

We lean towards one addition. Wheat beers are fermented warm, often 18 to 22 °C depending on the strain and the ester profile you want. That warmth carries yeast aroma forward strongly. A modest bitter base is all the hop needs to provide. If you want more hop aroma in a wheat beer, pick a variety with more to say and use it late.
Fresh hops matter more at low doses

Low alpha hops lose alpha acid as they age just as high alpha ones do, but the loss matters more because you are already using a lot of them. A packet that has spent a summer in a kitchen cupboard can lose a meaningful share of its bitterness and most of its aroma.

Buy small packets, keep them in the freezer and seal opened ones tightly with the air pressed out. In much of India a cupboard can sit above 30 °C for months, which is enough to turn a fresh floral hop into something that smells of old cheese. Rub a pellet before you brew. If the smell is flat or cheesy, use it only for bittering.

An IBU number on its own says little about how bitter a beer tastes. What matters is bitterness against malt. A quick check is the BU:GU ratio: IBU divided by the gravity points of the wort. A helles at 18 IBU and an original gravity of 1.046 has a ratio of 18 / 46, about 0.39. That is a soft, malt led balance. A weissbier at 12 IBU and 1.048 sits near 0.25, softer again.

Use the ratio when you change a recipe. If you brew a stronger helles at 1.052, keep the ratio near 0.39 and the target rises to about 20 IBU. Because Hersbrucker is low in alpha, that small change still means several extra grams at 60 minutes on a 20 litre batch, so recalculate rather than eyeball it.

The simplest way to learn this hop is a single malt, single hop helles: Pilsner malt, Hersbrucker and a clean lager yeast. Brew it at 18 IBU using the schedule above. Taste it alongside a wheat beer made with the same hop. Seeing how differently one hop reads in two styles is the start of designing hop bills rather than copying them.

Write down the alpha on your packet before you start, then recalculate the 60 minute addition with that number. That one habit fixes most of the bitterness surprises homebrewers have with German lagers.
faqs: It is often grouped with noble style German aroma hops, but the strict noble list usually names Hallertau Mittelfrüh, Tettnang, Spalt and Saaz. Hersbrucker shares their gentle floral and spicy profile.
How much Hersbrucker should I use in a helles?
For 20 litres at about 18 IBU, roughly 30 g at 60 minutes plus 15 g at 15 minutes, assuming 3.5% alpha. Recalculate with the alpha on your packet.
Should I dry hop a weissbier with Hersbrucker?
Usually not. Weissbier aroma comes from the yeast. A dry hop tends to compete with the banana and clove rather than add to them.
